chunks.title: Two and twenty
chunks.text: Consider this example for the 2 in 20 situation. Assume you're a hedge fund manager and that you've been managing a fund of $100 million, and that over the course of a year, your skill has resulted in an increase in value of that fund by 15%. So over that year, the fund grew in value from $100 million to $115 million.

chunks.title: Two and twenty
chunks.text: What would your compensation be? So it's 2% of AUM plus 20% of the profit. The 2 component works out to be $2 million. The 20 component is 20% of the $15 million profit we made, which is 3 million. So total compensation for this year for

chunks.title: Two and twenty
chunks.text: the hedge fund manager would be about $5 million. Now one question that some people might have is, hey, is this 2 component 2% of $100 million or 2% of $115? And it depends on the hedge fund, of course, and depends on when they take snapshots to do accounting.

chunks.title: Two and twenty
chunks.text: The full answer is probably it's going to be a blend somewhere between $100 million and $115 million. This structure 2 and 20 has been assailed lately. And it's very rare now to find a hedge fund that offers rates that high. They're much lower now, 1 and 10, things like that.

chunks.title: Two and twenty
chunks.text: So the 2 and 20 was in the heyday of hedge funds in the 90s and early 2000s. Nowadays they're typically a little bit lower. There are some star hedge funds that charge more. For instance, SAC Capital, which is no longer operating to the public anyways, that charge as much as 40%.

chunks.title: Two and twenty
chunks.text: So it was 4 and 40. However, most hedge funds you find today will be somewhere between 2 and 20 or lower.
